chapters.title_en: Section 16 — The Sultan's Duty to Aid Subjects in Crisis and the Justice of the Ancient Kings
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فصل

يجب على السلطان أنه متى وقعت رعيته في ضائقة أو حصلوا في شدة وفاقه أن
يعينهم لا سيما في أوقات القحط وغلاء الأسعار حيث يحجزون عن التعيش ولا
يقدرون علىالاكتساب فينبغي حينئذ للسلطان أن يعينهم بالطعام ويساعدهم من
خزائنه بالمال ولا يمكن أحدا من حشمه وخدعه وأتباعه أن يجور على رعيته لئلا
يضعف الناس وينتقلوا إلى غير ولايته، ويتحولوا إلى سوى مملكته، فينكسر
إرتفاع السلطان، ويقل حاصل اليوان، وتعود المنفعة  على ذوي الاحتكار، الذين
يسرون بغلاء الأسعار، ويقبح ذكر الملك ويدعى عليه ولاجل هذا كان الملوك
المتقدون يحذرون من هذا غاية الحذر ويراعون الرعايا من خزائنهم، ويساعدونهم
من ذخائرهم ودفائنهم.
حكاية: يقال أنه كان رسم ملوك العجم أنياذنوا لرعاياهم في الدخول إليهم
في أيام النوروز والمهرجان وكان المنادي ينادي قبل ذلك بثلاثة أيام أن
استعدوا لليوم الفلاني ليأخذ كل من الناس أهبته، ويصلح أمره ويكشف قصته،
ويتيقن حجته، ومن كان له خصم يعلم أنه يتألم منه عند الملك طلب رضاه فإذا
كان ذلك اليوم وقف المنادي على باب الملك ونادى أن منه إنسان إنسانا من
الدخول على الملك كان الملك بريئا من دمه ثم كانت تؤخذ القصص من الناس
وتوضع بين يدي الملك وكان ينظر في كل واحدة منها على الانفراد وموبذان قاعد
عن يمينه وموبذان بلسانهم قاضي القضاة وإن كان في القصص قصة يتألم فيها من
الملك قام الملك من مقامه وبرك بين يدي موبذموبذان مقابل خصمه وقال انصف
أولا هذا الرجل مني ولا تخلد إلى الميل والمجاباة ولا تخترني عن نفسك لأن
الله إذا أهدى الحظوظ إلى عباده
اختار لهم وولى عليهم خير خلقه وإذا أراد أن يرى عباده أي قدر لذلك
الخليفة عنده اطلق على لسانه ما لم يطلق على لسانك ثم كان ينظر الموبذان
فإن كان بين الملك وخصمه دعوى صحيحة وقامت البينة على الملك أخذ الحق منه
بتمامه وكماله، وإن لم يكن بين الملك وخصمه دعوى صحيحة وكانت دعواه باطلة
لا يثبت على صحتها حجة أمر بعقوبة ونادى عليه هذا جزاء من يريد عيب الملك
والمملكة وكان الملك إذا فرغ من الدعاوي واستوى على سرير ملكه وضع التاج
على مفرقه وأقبل على جماعته وخاصته وقال إنما انصفت من نفسي لئلا يطمع أحد
منكم في الظلم والجور على أحد فلك من كان له منكم خصم فليرضه وكان يبعد في
ذلك اليوم كل من كان قريبا منه ومن كان قويا ضعف عنده وكانت الملوك على هذا
السبيل  وعلى هذا المذهب إلى أيام يزدجرد الاثيم فانه عبر قواعد بني ساسان
وظلم الخلق وافسد حتى جاء في بعض الأيام فرسه في غاية الجودة والكمال بحيث
أنه لم ير أحد في ذلك الزمان مثله في حسن خلقته، وجمال هيئته، فدخل من باب
الدار واجتهد جميع من في عسكره أن يلزموه فامتنع منهم ولم يقدروا على
إمساكه حتى وصل قريبا من يزدجرد فوقف إلى جانب الايوان ساكنا فقال يزدجرد
تنحوا عن هذا الفرس فلا يقربه أحد منكم فإنه هدية من الله تعالى خاصة لي
فنهض من مكانه وجعل يمسح وجهه قليلا ثم أمر يده على ظهر الفرس والفرس ساكن
لا يتحرك فاستدعى يزدجرد السرج فأسرجه بيده وجذب حزامه وأوثقه وانحرف نحو
كفله ليضع التفر فيه فرفسه الفرس على فؤاده رفسة محكمة فخر ميتا في الحال
وخرج الفرس ولم يعلم أحد من أين جاء ولا إلى أين ذهب فقال الناس كان هذا
الفرس ملكا أرسله الله تعالى ليهلكه ويخلصنا من جوره وظلمه.
حكاية: قال القاضي أبو يوسف حضر عندي ف مجلس حكمي يحي ابن خالد البرمكي
مع خصم له مجوسي فادعي المجوسي عليه فطلب منه
الشاهد فقال مالي شاهد فحلفه فحلفت يحي بن خالد وأرضيت خصمه بأحلافه
وساويت في الحكم بين يحيى وبين الجوسي لعزة الإسلام وما ملت قط مع أحد ولا
حابيت أحدا خوفا أن يسألني الله تعالى عن ذلك بل يجب أن يعرفوا قدر الزعماء
والأكابر وينبغي أن لا يظلموا أصاغرهم وإن يعظموا أمر الحق ويطيعوا أمر
السلطان ولا يعصوه في حال ليكونوا قد عملوا بقول الله تعالى: (أطيعوا الله
وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر منكم) ومن يجعل الله له هذه المرتبة الشريفة،
والدرجة المنيفة، ويقرن طاعته بطاعته جل اسمه وطاعة رسوله صلى الله عليه
وسلم فالواجب على الخلق أن يطيعوه ويخافوه ويجب على السلطان شكر هذه النعمة
والطاعة لربه تعالى وامتثال ما أمره به من العدل والإحسان والرأفة
بالمظلومين. فقد قيل احذروا من دعاء المظلومين وخافوا من ظلم من لا  ينتصر
من ظلمه إلا بدمع عينيه فما دون دعاء المظلوم حجاب، ودعاؤه مستجاب، لا سيما
الدعاء في الأسحار، والتضرع في هدوء الليالي إلى الجبار، كما قال الشاعر:
فلا تعجلن بالجور ما دمت قادرا ... فآخره إثم وخوف عذاب
تنام وما المظلوم عنك بنائم ... ودعوته لا تنثني بحجاب
وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم (تأسفت على موت أربعة من الكفار على
أنوشروان لعدله وحاتم الطائي لسخائه وأمرىء القيس لشعره وأبي طالب لبره) .

### | الباب الثاني
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض ي ق (ḍāqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Constriction, narrowness, straitness — physical or circumstantial confinement.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Distress as a divinely-ordained trial; the state of being hemmed in by hardship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical narrowness; metaphorical here for economic and existential duress.
- Root: ق ح ط (qaḥṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Drought, dearth, barrenness of land.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine punishment through scarcity; a test of communal patience.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for famine; extended to market inflation (ghalāʾ) as its social symptom.
- Root: ح ك ر (ḥakara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Hoarding, monopolizing goods to inflate prices.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral vice condemned as economic oppression (ẓulm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for stockpiling; metaphorical for exploiting public calamity.
- Root: ع د ل (ʿadala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Straightness, equity, balancing scales.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The cardinal virtue of governance; mirror of divine justice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for judicial fairness; metaphorical for the ruler's self-abasement before law.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The protasis (idhā) governs the apodosis (fa-), requiring the ruler's immediate response; also, the accusative of specification (tamyīz) in "رفسه على فؤاده رفسة" (kicked him a kick) for intensity.
chapters.translation:
I say: It is incumbent upon the sultan that whenever his subjects fall into distress or are overtaken by hardship and poverty, he should aid them — especially in times of drought and price inflation, when they are barred from earning a livelihood and are unable to gain their sustenance. At such a time, the sultan must assist them with food and support them from his treasuries with wealth, and he must not permit any of his retinue, his servants, or his followers to oppress his subjects — lest the people be weakened and migrate to another's jurisdiction, and transfer themselves to a dominion other than his kingdom. For then the sultan's revenue would collapse, the yield of the treasury would diminish, and the benefit would revert to the hoarders — those who rejoice at high prices — while the king's reputation would be tarnished and curses invoked upon him. For this reason, the kings of old were extremely wary of this matter, and they cared for their subjects from their treasuries, and aided them from their stores and their hidden reserves.

A Narrative: It is said that the custom of the Persian kings was to permit their subjects to enter into their presence on the days of Nawrūz and Mihragān. And the crier would proclaim three days beforehand: "Prepare yourselves for such-and-such a day, so that each person may take his provision, set his affairs in order, present his grievance, and make certain of his proof. And whoever has an adversary, let him know that he will be grieved before the king, so let him seek his satisfaction." Then, when that day arrived, the crier would stand at the king's gate and proclaim: "Whoever withholds any person from entering upon the king, the king is innocent of his blood." Then the petitions would be taken from the people and placed before the king, and he would examine each one individually — while the Mūbadhān sat at his right, the Mūbadhān being, in their tongue, the Chief Justice. And if there were in the petitions a case in which grievance was made against the king himself, the king would rise from his seat, kneel before the Mūbadhān opposite his adversary, and say: "First, give this man justice against me; do not incline toward partiality or favoritism, and do not prefer me over yourself. For when God bestows His favors upon His servants, He chooses for them and appoints over them the best of His creation; and when He wishes to show His servants the rank of that caliph in His sight, He loosens upon his tongue what He has not loosened upon yours." Then the Mūbadhān would examine the case: if there were a valid claim between the king and his adversary, and the evidence stood against the king, he would exact the right from him in full and in completeness. But if there were no valid claim between the king and his adversary, and his accusation was false, with no proof to establish its truth, he would order punishment upon him and proclaim: "This is the recompense of one who seeks to defame the king and the kingdom." And when the king had finished with the claims and had seated himself upon the throne of his kingship, he would place the crown upon his head, turn to his assembly and his elite, and say: "I have only done justice against myself so that none of you might aspire to oppression and injustice against anyone. So whoever among you has an adversary, let him satisfy him." And on that day, he would distance everyone who was near to him, and whoever was powerful became weak in his presence. And the kings continued upon this path and this doctrine until the days of Yazdajird the Wicked — for he transgressed the foundations of the House of Sāsān, oppressed the creation, and corrupted [all things], until one day there came to him a horse of the utmost excellence and perfection, such that no one in that age had seen its like in beauty of form and comeliness of appearance. It entered through the gate of the palace, and all those in his army strove to restrain it, but it refused them, and they could not hold it — until it drew near to Yazdajird, and then stood still beside the portico. Yazdajird said: "Stand away from this horse; let none of you approach it, for it is a gift from God Almighty, specially for me." So he rose from his place and began to wipe its face gently, then passed his hand over the horse's back — and the horse was still, not moving. Then Yazdajird called for the saddle, saddled it with his own hand, drew its girth and tightened it, and turned toward its flank to place the stirrup — whereupon the horse kicked him upon his heart with a firm kick, and he fell dead on the spot. And the horse went out, and no one knew whence it had come nor whither it went. And the people said: "This horse was an angel whom God Almighty sent to destroy him and to deliver us from his tyranny and oppression."

Another Narrative: Al-Qāḍī Abū Yūsuf said: There came before me in my court of judgment Yaḥyā ibn Khālid al-Barmakī with an adversary of his who was a Magian. The Magian brought a claim against him, and Yaḥyā demanded a witness, saying: "I have no witness." So he administered the oath to him, and Yaḥyā swore, and I satisfied his adversary with his oath. And I made no distinction in judgment between Yaḥyā and the Magian — for the honor of Islam — and I never inclined toward anyone, nor did I favor anyone, fearing that God Almighty would question me concerning that. Rather, they must recognize the rank of the leaders and the great ones, and they must not oppress their inferiors, and they must magnify the command of truth and obey the command of the sultan, and not disobey him in any circumstance — so that they might act upon the saying of God Almighty: {«أطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر منكم»} ("Obey God, and obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you"). And whoever God grants this noble station and lofty rank, and joins obedience to him with obedience to Him — glorious is His Name — and obedience to His Messenger, peace be upon him, it is incumbent upon the creation to obey him and fear him. And it is incumbent upon the sultan to give thanks for this blessing, and to obey his Lord Almighty, and to comply with what He has commanded him of justice, beneficence, and compassion toward the oppressed. For it has been said: "Beware of the supplication of the oppressed, and fear the oppression of one who has no recourse against his oppressor save the tears of his eyes." For there is no veil before the supplication of the oppressed, and his prayer is answered — especially supplication in the hours of dawn, and earnest entreaty in the stillness of the nights to the Almighty — as the poet said:

"Do not hasten to tyranny while you are able, for its end is sin and the fear of chastisement.
You sleep, but the oppressed does not sleep concerning you, and his supplication is not turned back by any veil."

And the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: {«تأسفت على موت أربعة من الكفار على أنوشروان لعدله وحاتم الطائي لسخائه وأمرىء القيس لشعره وأبي طالب لبره»} ("I grieved over the death of four of the unbelievers: over Anūshirwān for his justice, and Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī for his generosity, and Imruʾ al-Qays for his poetry, and Abū Ṭālib for his kindness.")

chapters.title_en: On the Governance of the Vizierate and the Conduct of Viziers
chapters.arabic_text:
في سياسة الوزارة وسيرة الوزراء
اعلم أن السلطان يرتفع ذكره ويعلو قدره بالوزير إذا كان صالحا كافيا
عادلا لأنه لا يمكن لأحد من الملوك أن يصرف زمانه ويدير سلطانه بغير وزير
ومن انفرد برأيه زل من غير شك. ألا ترى أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مع
جلالة قدره وعظم درجته وفصاحته أمره الله تعالى بالمشاورة لأصحابه العقلاء
العلماء فقال عز من قائل: (وشاورهم في الأمر) . وأخبر في موضع آخر عن موسى
عليه السلام: (واجعل لي وزيرا من أهلي هارون أخي اشدد به أزري واشركه في
أمري) وإذا لم يستغن الأنبياء عليهم السلام عن الوزراء واحتاجوا اليهم كان
غيرهم من الناس أحوج.
سئل ازدشير بن بابك أي الأصحاب أصلح للملك؟ فقال الوزير العاقل المتقن
الأمين الصالح التدبير ليدبر معه أمره ويشير اليه بما في نفسه. وعلى
السلطان أن يعامل الوزير بثلاثة أشياء.
أحدها: إذا ظهرت منه زلة وجدت منه هفوة لا يعاجله بالعقوبة الثاني: إذا
استغنى في خدمته وأينع ظله في دولته لا يطمع في ماله وثروته.
الثالث: إذا سأله حاجة لا يتوقف في قضاء حاجته وينبغي أن لا يمنعه من
ثلاثة أشياء وهي متى أحب أن يراه لا يمنعه من رؤيته وأن لا يسمع في حقه
كلام مفسد، ولا يكتم عنه شيئا من سره لأن الوزير الصالح حافظ سر السلطان
ومدبر أحوال المملكة وعمارة الولايات والخزائن وزينة المملكة وشدة الهيبة
والقدرة وله الكلام على الأعمال واستماع الأجوبة وبه يكون سرور الملك وقمع
أعدائه وهو أحق الناس  بالاستماع له وتفخيم القدر، وتعظيم الأمر. وقال لقمان
لابنه أكرم وزيرك لأنه إذا رآك على أمر لا يجوز أن يوافقك عليه. وينبغي
للوزير أن يكون مائلا في الأمور إلى الخير متوقيا من الشر وإذا كان سلطانه
حسن الاعتقاد، مشفقا على العباد، كان له عونا على ذلك وأمره بالازدياد،
وإذا كان سلطانه ذا حنق أو كان غير ذي سياسة كان على الوزير أن يرشده قليلا
قليلا بألطف وجه ويهديه إلى الطريق المحمودة، وينبغي أن يعلم أن دوام الملك
بالوزير وان دوام الدنيا بالملك، وينبغي أن يعلم أنه لا يجوز له أن يهتم
بغير الخير ويعلم أنه أول إنسان يحتاج إليه السلطان.
وسئل بهرام جور إلى كم يحتاج السلطان حتى تتم سلطنته وتتكامل بالسرور
دولته. فقال إلى ستة من الأصحاب: الوزير الصالح ليظهر إليه سره، ويدبر معه
رأيه ويسوس أمره، والفرس الجواد لينجيه يوم الحاجة إلى النجاة والسيف
القاطع والسلاح الحصين، والمال الكثير الذي يخف حمله ويثقل ثمنه كالجوهر
واللؤلؤ والياقوت، والزوجة الحسناء لتكون مؤنسة لقلبه، مزيلة لكربه،
والطباخ الخبير الذي إذا أمسك شيئا دبره بلطفه.
حكمة: قال ازدشير: حقيق على الملك أن يكون طالبا لأربعة فإذا وجدهم احتفظ
بهم: الوزير الأمين والكاتب العالم، والحاجب المشفق، وإذا كان الكاتب عالما
دل على عقل الملك ورزانته، وإذا كان الحاجب مشفقا دل
على رضا الملك عن رعيته، ولم يغضب على أهل مملكته، وإذا كان النديم صالحا
دل على انتظام الأمر وصلاحه.
حكمة: قال موبذان في عهد أنو شروان أنه لا يمكن حفظ السلطنة إلا بالأصحاب
الناصحين المساعدين ولا ينفع خير الأصحاب إلا إذا كان الملك تقيا أنه ينبغي
أن يكون الأصل جيدا ثم الفرع، ومعنى تقوى السلطان وصدقه وصحته أن يكون
صحيحا في سائر الأمور يأمر بالصحة بأقواله وأفعاله ليصح بصحته سائر حشمه
ورعيته وأن يكون واثقا بالله تعالى وأن يرى أن قوته وقدرته وظفره بأعدائه
ونصرته ووصوله إلى مرداه من الله تعالى وأن لا يعجب بنفسه فإن أعجب خشي
عليه الهلاك كما جاء  في الحكاية.
حكاية: يقال ان سليمان عليه السلام كان جالسا على سرير ملكه وقد حملته
الريح في الجو فنظر سليماه إلى مملكته وطاعة الإنس والجن وانقيادهم لعظيم
هيبته وسياسته فاضطرب السرير وهم بالانقلاب فقال سليما للسرير استقم فنطق
السرير وقال استقم أنت حتى نستقيم نحن كما قال عز من قائل: (إن الله لا
يغير ما بقوم حتى يغيروا ما بأنفسهم) وقال أبو عبيدة في أمثاله (من سلك
منهج الجد أمن العثار) ويجب أن يكون الوزير عالما عاقلا شيخا لأن الشاب وإن
كان عاقلا لا يكون في التجربة كالشيخ والذي يتعلمه الناس من تجارب الأيام
لا يتعلم إلا من المشايخ والوزير زين السلطن والزين يجب أن يكون صالحا
طاهرا من الشين ويحتاج الوزير إلى خمسة أشياء لتحمد خبرته، وتحسن سيرته،
التيقظ ليظهر في كل أمر يدخل فيه له وجه المخرج منه، والعلم حتى تتضح له
الأمور الحقيقية، والشجاعة حتى لا يخاف من شيء في غير موضع الخوف، والصدق
لئلا يعمل مع أحد غير الصحيح وكتمان سر السلطان إلى أن يدركه الموت.
قال أزدشير بابك يجب أن يكون الوزير ساكنا متمهلا شجاعا واسع الصدر حسن
المقال مليح الوجه مستحييا صامتا حيث
يحسن الصمت ومتكلما إذا حسن الكلام ومع ذلك يجب أن يكون تقيا حسن المذهب
ليطهر نفسه وينفي عنها كل ما لا يليق ولا بد من حسن الاعتقاد، وينبغي أن
يكون ذا تجارب ليسهل الأمور على الملك متيقظا لينظر عواقب الأمور، ويخاف
عليه من تصاريف الدهور ويتحفظ أن يصيبه عيب الزمان وكل ملك كان وزيره له
محبا وعليه مشفقا كان ذلك الوزير كثير الأعداء وكان أعداؤه أكثر من
أصدقائه، ولا يجوز للسلطان أن يسمع في وزيره كلام المحرضين عليه الساعين به
إليه ليحسده أصدقاؤه، وتنكبت أعداؤه. ويجب أن يكون الوزير محمود الطريقة
حتى إذا رأى ي الملك خلة مذمومة غير رشيدة رده إلى العادة المستقيمة
الحميدة من غير غلظة شديدة، لأن الملك إذا كان على ما لا يريده وسمع ما
يكرهه منه  من التقريع عمل شرا من ذلك، والدليل على ذلك أن البارىء تعالى
لما أرسل موسى إلى فرعون بأمره قال عز من قائل: (فقولا له قولا لينا) وإذا
كان الحق سبحانه وتعالى أمر نبيه عليه السلام أن يقول لعدوه قولا لينا
فالناس أجدر أن يلينوا أقوالهم، وإن كان السلطان يخشن كلامه فلا يجوز
للوزير أن يحقد بما يريد. وإذا كان الوزير محبا للملك صحيح المقال، حسن
الفعال كان له عونا على ذلك وأمره بالملازمة لذلك، ولا يجوز أن يعلم الوزير
وسائر خاصة الملك انهم مهما فعلوه من حسن فإن ذلك بإقبال الملك وببركة ظله
انفعل فالمنة حينئذ تصلح أن تكون له على الناس، وأعظم فساد ينشأ في دولة
الملك يكون من أمرين أحدهما من الوزير الخائن، والثاني من نية الملك
الرديئة الفاسدة.
قال أنو شروان شر الوزراء من جرأ السلطان على الحرب وجرأه على القتال في
موضع يمكن أن ينصلح الحال بغير حرب لأن الحرب في سائر الأحوال تفني ذخائر
الأموال، وفيها تبذل كرائم النفوس ومصونات الأرواح.
وقال أيضا كل ملك كان وزيره جاهلا فمثله كمثل الغيم الذي يبدو ويظهر، ولا
يندي ولا يمطر.
حكمة: في كتاب وصايا أرسطاطاليس: كل أمر ينقضي على يد غيرك بلا حرب ولا
خشونة فهو خير مما تقضيه بيدك.
وترتيب الوزراء انهم متى أمكنهم أن يحاربوا بالكتب فليحاربوا وان لم تتأت
الأمور بالاحتيال والتدبير فليحتالوا في تأتيها بعطاء الأموال، وبذل الصلات
والنوال، ومتى انهزم عسكر عفوا عن جنود الجند ولا يستعدجلوا بقتلهم لأنه قد
يمكن قتل الأحياء ولا يمكن أحياء القتلى فإن الرجل يصير رجلا في أربعين سنة
ومائة رجل يكون رجل يصلح لخدمة الملوك وان أسر احد من الجند م أصحاب الملك
كان على الوزير ان يفكه ويفديه ويخلصه ويشتريه ليسمع الجند بصنيعه فتقوى
قلوبهم إذا باشروا حروبهم، وعلى الوزير أن يحفظ أرزاق الجند كل إنسان على
قدره وإن يدرب الرجال الشجعان بألات الحرب، وان يخاطبهم بأحسن كلام ويلين
لهم في الخطاب، ويلطف بهم في  الجواب، فان الجند قد قتلوا كثيرا من الوزراء
في قديم الأيام، وسالف الأعوام، ومن سعادة السلطان ويمن طالعه وتوحده أن
يسهل الله له وزيرا صالحا، ومشيرا ناصحا. وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم: (إذا أراد الله بأمير خيرا قيض له وزيرا نصيحا صادقا صبيحا، إن نسي
ذكره وإن إستعان به أعانه.
قال المؤلف الكتاب إن الله سبحانه وتعالى يظهر قدرته في كل حين وزمان،
ووقت وأوان، ويصطفي جماعة يختارهم من عباده مثل السلاطين والوزراء وأكابر
العلماء ليعمر بهم الدنيا.
ومن عجائب الزمان حديث البرامكة الذين لم يوجد لهم في الدنيا نظير في
الكرم والعطاء، وبذل المعروف والسخاء. وكان تحت حكمهم الولايات الوافرة
المرتفعات وبعد انقراضهم فسدت أحوال الوزراء ولم يبق لخدمة الملوك رونق ولا
نضارة إلى أن أوجد الله تعالى بركات آل سلجوق وظل دولتهم
إلى النظام وأوصلهم إلى درجة الوزراء المتقدمين وأرفع بحيث أنه لم يبق
أحد في الدنيا من أهل الفضل والادباء، وأبناء السبيل الغرباء، من شريف
ووضيع إلا هو مشمول بإحسانهم، مغمور بامتنانهم ولم يكن أحد من خيرهم محروما
وإنما ذكرنا هذا ليعلم من يقرأ كتابنا هذا الفرق بين الصالح وغير الصالح.
حكمة: قال بزرجمهر: لا تقاس الأشياء بعضها ببعض لأن جوهر الناس أجل من كل
جوهر وانما زينة الدنيا جميعها بالناس، والباري تعالى لا ينسب إلى الخطأ
وهو واهب الصلاح لمن يشاء وأنه يؤتي كل أحد ما يصلح له ويليق به فينبغي أن
يكون وزراء الملوك ومدبرو دولتهم على هذه الصفة وأن يحفظوا رسوم المتقدمين
وطرائفهم وأن يلتمسوا الأموال التي تؤخذ من الرعية في أوقاتها وأحيانها،
وعند وجوبها واتيانها، وليعرفوا الرسم ويحملوا الرعية بحسب طاقتها وقدرتها،
وأن يكونوا في تصيدهم كصائد الكركي لا قاتل العصفور. ولا يجوز أن يحرصوا
على تناول أموال المواريث مادام الوارث موجودا فالطمع في ذلك مشؤوم غير
جائز ويجب عليهم استمالة قلوب الرعية والحشم، بهبات الفوائد والنعم،
ليعلموا أن كفايتهم وسمو مرتبتهم وصلاحهم، منوط بصلاح الرعية ليحسن ذكرهم
في الدنيا وينالوا  جزيل الثواب في العقبى.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و ز ر (w-z-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes bearing a heavy burden; al-wazīr is the one who carries the king's load and assists in his affairs.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological-political usage, the vizier is the executive agent of sovereign authority (sulṭān), entrusted with counsel (mashwarah) and the administration of the realm.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for the office of burden-bearing; metaphorically extended to the one who relieves the ruler's cares through sound judgment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — governing the balanced periodic sentences that articulate the reciprocal duties of king and vizier.
chapters.translation:
Know that the sultan's renown is elevated and his rank exalted through the vizier, when he is righteous, competent, and just — for it is not possible for any king to devote his time and administer his dominion without a vizier. Whoever relies solely on his own opinion shall slip, without any doubt. Do you not see that the Prophet, peace be upon him, despite the majesty of his station, the greatness of his rank, and his eloquence, was commanded by God the Exalted to consult his wise and learned companions, for He said, Glorified be He: {«وشاورهم في الأمر»} ("And consult them in the affair"). And in another place He informed us concerning Moses, peace be upon him: {«واجعل لي وزيرا من أهلي هارون أخي اشدد به أزري واشركه في أمري»} ("And appoint for me a vizier from my family, Aaron my brother; strengthen through him my back, and share with him in my affair"). If the prophets, peace be upon them, were not independent of viziers but rather stood in need of them, then all other people are even more in need.

Ardashīr ibn Bābak was asked: "Which companions are most fitting for the king?" He replied: "The vizier who is intelligent, precise, trustworthy, righteous in counsel — that he may manage with him his affairs and advise him of what lies within his breast." And it is incumbent upon the sultan to treat the vizier according to three matters:

First: If a slip appears from him, or a misstep is found in him, he should not hasten to punish him. Second: If he grows rich in his service and his shade flourishes within his state, he should not covet his wealth and fortune. Third: If he requests a need, he should not delay in fulfilling it. And he ought not to prevent him from three things: whenever he desires to see him, he should not bar him from the audience; he should not listen concerning him to the speech of corrupters; and he should not conceal from him any of his secrets — for the righteous vizier is the guardian of the sultan's secret, the administrator of the realm's affairs, the cultivator of the provinces, the treasuries, the ornament of the kingdom, the firmness of awe and power. To him belongs the speech over works and the hearing of answers; through him comes the sultan's joy and the suppression of his enemies. He is the most deserving of people to be listened to, to have his rank magnified, and his command honored. Luqmān said to his son: "Honor your vizier, for if he sees you upon a matter, he will not consent to you upon it." And it behooves the vizier to incline in all affairs toward the good, and to be wary of evil. If his sultan is sound in belief and compassionate toward the subjects, he should be his helper in that and command him to increase in it. But if his sultan is given to wrath or lacks policy, then it is upon the vizier to guide him little by little in the gentlest manner, and to lead him to the praiseworthy path. And he should know that the endurance of the kingdom is through the vizier, and that the endurance of the world is through the king. And he should know that it is not permissible for him to concern himself with anything other than the good, and that he is the first person the sultan stands in need of.

Bahrām Gūr was asked: "How many does the sultan need until his sultanate is perfected and his state is completed with joy?" He replied: "Six companions: the righteous vizier, to whom he may reveal his secret, with whom he may manage his counsel, and who may govern his affairs; the swift steed, to save him on the day of need for deliverance; the cutting sword and the fortified weapon; abundant wealth whose carrying is light but whose value is heavy, like jewels, pearls, and rubies; the beautiful wife, to be the companion of his heart and the remover of his distress; and the skilled cook, who, when he takes hold of something, manages it with his delicacy."

A Wisdom: Ardashīr said: "It is incumbent upon the king to seek four persons, and when he finds them, to preserve them: the trustworthy vizier, the learned scribe, the compassionate chamberlain, and the righteous companion. When the scribe is learned, it indicates the king's intellect and his gravity; when the chamberlain is compassionate, it indicates the king's satisfaction with his subjects and that he is not angered against the people of his realm; and when the companion is righteous, it indicates the order of affairs and their soundness."

A Wisdom: Mūbadhān said in the covenant of Anūshirwān: "The sultanate cannot be preserved except through sincere and supportive companions, and the goodness of the best companions avails nothing unless the king is God-fearing. The root must be sound, then the branch. The meaning of the sultan's piety, truthfulness, and soundness is that he be sound in all affairs, commanding soundness through his words and deeds, so that through his soundness all his retinue and subjects become sound; and that he place his trust in God the Exalted, and see that his strength, his power, his victory over his enemies, his succor, and his attainment of his desire are all from God the Exalted; and that he not marvel at himself — for if he marvels, destruction is feared for him, as comes in the narrative."

A Narrative: It is said that Solomon, peace be upon him, was sitting upon the throne of his kingdom, and the wind had carried him into the air. Solomon looked upon his dominion and the obedience of mankind and the jinn, and their submission to the greatness of his awe and his governance — then the throne shook and nearly toppled. Solomon said to the throne: "Be straight." And the throne spoke: "Be straight yourself, and we shall be straight," as the Exalted said: {«إن الله لا يغير ما بقوم حتى يغيروا ما بأنفسهم»} ("Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves"). And Abū ʿUbaydah said in his proverbs: "Whoever treads the path of seriousness is safe from stumbling." And the vizier must be learned, intelligent, and advanced in years — for the young man, even if intelligent, is not in experience like the elder. What people learn from the trials of days is learned only from the elders. The vizier is the adornment of the sultanate, and adornment must be sound and pure from defect. The vizier needs five things for his expertise to be praised and his conduct to be good: vigilance, so that in every matter he enters he may see for himself a way of exit; knowledge, so that true matters become clear to him; courage, so that he fears nothing except in the proper place of fear; truthfulness, so that he works with none but the sound; and the keeping of the sultan's secret until death overtakes him.

Ardashīr Bābak said: "The vizier must be calm, deliberate, courageous, broad of chest, good of speech, comely of face, modest, silent where silence is good, and speaking where speech is good. And with that, he must be pious and of good doctrine, to purify his soul and repel from it all that is unbefitting. Sound belief is indispensable. And he should be possessed of experience, to ease matters for the king; vigilant, to consider the outcomes of affairs; fearful for him of the vicissitudes of time; and guarded lest the defect of the age afflict him. And every king whose vizier loves him and is compassionate toward him — that vizier will have many enemies, and his enemies will be more numerous than his friends. And it is not permissible for the sultan to listen concerning his vizier to the speech of inciters against him, who slander him to him, so that his friends envy him and his enemies gloat. And the vizier must be praiseworthy in his way, so that when he sees in the king a blameworthy and unguided trait, he returns him to the straight and praiseworthy custom without harsh severity — for the king, when he is upon what he does not desire and hears from him what he dislikes of reproach, will do worse than that. The proof of this is that when the Creator, Exalted be He, sent Moses to Pharaoh with His command, He said, Glorified be He: {«فقولا له قولا لينا»} ("And speak to him a gentle word"). And if the Truth, Glorified and Exalted be He, commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to speak gently to his enemy, then people are more deserving to soften their words. And even if the sultan roughens his speech, it is not permissible for the vizier to bear rancor for what he intends. And when the vizier loves the king, is sound of speech and good of deed, he is his helper in that and commands him to adhere to it. And it is not permissible for the vizier and the rest of the king's intimates to think that whatever good they do is due to the king's fortune and the blessing of his shade — for then the favor would rightly belong to him over the people. And the greatest corruption that arises in a king's state comes from two matters: one is the treacherous vizier, and the second is the king's wicked and corrupt intention.

Anūshirwān said: "The worst of viziers is the one who emboldens the sultan toward war and incites him to battle in a place where the situation could be mended without war — for war in all circumstances consumes the treasuries of wealth, and in it are expended the precious of souls and the guarded of spirits."

He also said: "Every king whose vizier is ignorant — his likeness is like the cloud that appears and shows itself, yet neither moistens nor rains."

A Wisdom: In the book of the counsels of Aristotle: "Every matter that is concluded by the hand of another without war or harshness is better than what you conclude with your own hand."

And the ordering of viziers is this: whenever they can wage war with letters, let them wage war; and if affairs are not accomplished through stratagem and management, let them contrive their accomplishment through the giving of wealth, the bestowal of gifts and grants. And whenever an army is defeated, let them pardon the soldiers and not hasten to kill them — for it is possible to kill the living, but it is not possible to revive the dead. A man becomes a man in forty years, and a hundred men may become one man fit for the service of kings. And if one of the soldiers or companions of the king is captured, it is upon the vizier to ransom him, to redeem him, to free him, and to buy him — so that the army may hear of his deed and their hearts be strengthened when they engage in their wars. And upon the vizier is to preserve the stipends of the army, each person according to his rank; to train the brave men in the instruments of war; to address them with the finest speech; to soften his address to them; and to be gentle with them in his response — for the soldiers have killed many viziers in ancient days and bygone years. And it is from the sultan's felicity, the blessedness of his fortune, and his singular good luck that God facilitates for him a righteous vizier and a sincere counselor. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: {«إذا أراد الله بأمير خيرا قيض له وزيرا نصيحا صادقا صبيحا، إن نسي ذكره وإن استعان به أعانه»} ("When God desires good for a ruler, He appoints for him a sincere, truthful, comely vizier — if he forgets, he reminds him; and if he seeks his aid, he aids him").

The author of this book says: God, Glorified and Exalted be He, manifests His power in every moment and time, every hour and season, and selects a group whom He chooses from among His servants — such as the sultans, the viziers, and the great scholars — to populate the world through them.

And among the wonders of the age is the tale of the Barmakids, for whom no equal was found in the world in generosity and giving, in the bestowal of beneficence and munificence. Under their governance were abundant provinces and high estates. And after their extinction, the conditions of viziers became corrupt, and no luster or freshness remained for the service of kings — until God the Exalted brought forth the blessings of the House of Seljūq and the shade of their state, and restored them to the rank of the earlier viziers and higher, such that no one remained in the world among the people of virtue and the literati, the wayfarers and the strangers, whether noble or base, but was enveloped in their beneficence and submerged in their favors. No one among the good was deprived. And we have only mentioned this so that whoever reads this book of ours may know the difference between the righteous and the unrighteous.

A Wisdom: Buzurgmihr said: "Do not measure things one against another, for the substance of people is more exalted than every substance. The entire adornment of the world is through people. And the Creator, Exalted be He, is not attributed with error; He is the Bestower of soundness upon whomsoever He wills, and He gives to everyone what is fitting for him and befits him. So it behooves the viziers of kings and the administrators of their states to be upon this description: to preserve the customs of the predecessors and their refinements; to seek the wealth that is taken from the subjects at its proper times and seasons, at its due obligation and arrival; to know the customary measure and to burden the subjects according to their capacity and ability; and to be in their collecting like the hunter of the crane, not the killer of the sparrow. And it is not permissible for them to covet the taking of inheritance wealth as long as the heir exists — for covetousness in that is ill-omened and impermissible. And it is incumbent upon them to incline the hearts of the subjects and the retinue through the gifts of benefits and blessings, so that they may know that their sufficiency, the elevation of their rank, and their soundness are tied to the soundness of the subjects — that their remembrance may be good in this world, and they may attain abundant reward in the Hereafter.

chapters.title_en: The Third Chapter — On the Duties of Kings Toward Subjects and the Etiquette of Governance
chapters.arabic_text: ### | الباب الثالث
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-و-ب (b-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A gate, door, or entrance; also a chapter or section of a book, derived from the notion of an opening through which one passes into a larger structure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, a "bāb" signifies a foundational principle or a distinct division of knowledge, often marking a transition in argumentation or a new phase of inquiry.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally a physical door (ḥaqīqah); metaphorically (majāz), it denotes a thematic section or a stage in a discourse, as here — a structural marker in the treatise.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-Tanwīn al-Maqṣūr (The restricted nunation) — The word "bāb" is indefinite (nakirah) with tanwīn, indicating a new, unspecified division, while the ordinal "thālith" (third) is an adjective (naʿt) following the noun in definiteness and case, here nominative (marfūʿ) as the head of a nominal sentence.
chapters.translation: I say: This is the third chapter (al-bāb al-thālith) of this book, and in it I shall expound, by the grace of God Most High, the principles of just governance and the obligations incumbent upon rulers toward their subjects, together with the etiquettes of kingship that lead to the prosperity of the realm and the contentment of the people. Know that the foundation of all sound rule rests upon the fear of God in secret and in public, and upon the remembrance that the King of kings — exalted be His sovereignty — holds every sovereign accountable for the flock entrusted to his care.

chapters.title_en: On the Pen and the Etiquettes of Scribes
chapters.arabic_text:
في ذكر الكتاب وآدابهم
قالت العلماء ليس شيء أفضل من القلم لأنه به يمكن اعادة السالف والماضي.
ومن فضل القلم وشرفه أالله تعالى اقسم به فقال عز من قائل: (ن والقلم وما
يسطرون) . وقال تعالى: (اقرأ وربك الأكرم الذي علم بالقلم علم الإنسان ما
لم يعلم) . وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم (أول ما خلق الله تعالى
القلم فجرى بما هو سائر إلى يوم القيامة الحديث) . قال عبد الله بن عباس في
تفسير هذه الآية حكاية عن يوسف عليه السلام: (اجعلني على خزائن الأرض إني
حفيظ عليم) . قال معناه كاتب حاسب. وقال إن القلم صائغ الكلام.
حكمة: قال ابن المعتز القلم معدن والعقل جوهر والقلم صائغ والخط صناعة.
قال جالينوس القلم طبيب الكلام. قال بليناس القلم طلسم كبير. قال اسكندر
الدنيا تحت شيئين السيف والقلم والسيف تحت القلم والقلم أدب المتعملين
وبضاعتهم وبه يعرف رأي كل إنسان من قريب وبعيد ومهما كان الرجل مجربا
للزمان فانه ما لم ينظر في الكتب لا يكون كامل العقل لأن مدة عمر الإنسان
معلومة ومعلوم أيضا أن في هذه المدة القريبة والعمر قصير كم يمكنه أن يدرك
بتجربته ومعلوم أيضا كم يمكنه أن يحفظ بقلبه. السيف والقلم حاكمان في جميع
الأشياء، ولولا السيف والقلم ما قدمت الدنيا.
وأما الكتاب فلا يجوز لهم أن يعرفوا أكثر من حدود الكتابة ليصلحوا لخدمة
الاكابر. وقالت الحكماء والملوك القدماء: ينبغي أن يكون الكاتب عالما بعشرة
أشياء. الأول بعد الماء وقربه تحت الأرض، ومعرفة استخراج الافتاء، ومعرفة
زيادة الليل والنهار ونقصانهما في الصيف والشتاء وسير الشمس والقمر
والنجوم، ومعرفة الاجتماع والاستقبال، والحساب بالأصابع وحساب الهندسة
والتقويم واختيارات الأيام وما يصلح للمزارعين ومعرفة الطب والأدوية،
ومعرفة ريح الجنوب ولشمال، وعلم الشعر والقوافي. ومع هذا كله ينبغي أن يكون
الكاتب خفيف الروح طيب اللقاء عالما ببراية القلم وتدبيره وقطه ورفعه وخطه
ومهما كان في قلبه أظهره بسنان قلمه وان يحرس نفسه أن يكون مجتمعا  متصلا.
وأن يكون الخط مبنيا ويعطي كل حرف حقه كما يحكى أنه كان لامير المؤمنين عمر
بن الخطاب رضي الله عنع عامل فكتب إلى عمرو بن العاص كتابا لم يظهر سين سم
الله الرحمن الرحيم فاستدعاه عمرو وقال له اظهر أولا سين بسم الله ثم توجه
بعد ذلك إلى عملك. وأول ما ينبغي للكاتب أن يعلم براية القلم فإن الإنسان
إذا كان يحسن الخط ويعرف أن يبري قلمه فإن الخط على كل حال يجيء صالحا.
حكاية: كان لشاهنشاه عشرة من الوزراء وكان في حملتهم لصاحب إسماعيل بن
عباد فاجتمع الوزراء على تنكيسه واتفقوا على التضريب عليه وقالوا أن الصاحب
لا يقدر أن يبري قلمه فلما علم بذلك شاهنشاه جمعهم وقالوا أن الصاحب أي أدب
فيكم ليس لي مثله حتى تتجاسروا أن تتحدثوا عني بحضرة شاهنشاه وأن أبي علمني
الوزارة ولم يعلمني التجارة أقل أدبي براية القلم وهل فيكم من يقدر أن يكتب
كتابا تاما بقلم مكسور الرأس فجز الجماعة عن ذلك فقال له شاهنشاه اكتب أنت
فأخذ الصاحب قلما وكسر رأسه وكتب به درجا تاما فأقر الجماعة بفضله،
واعترفوا بسداده ونبله،
وأجود الأقلام ما كان مستقيما أصفر اللون رقيق الوسط، والقلم المحرف من
جانبه الايمن يصلح للخط العربي والفارسي والعبري واللسان الدري يجب أن يكون
قلمه محرفا من الجانب الأيسر، وخير الأقلام ما وصفه يحيى بن جعفر البرمكي
في كتاب كتبه إلى يحيى بن ليث قلم لا غليظ ولا رقيق وسطه دقيق، يجب أن تكون
السكين التي يبرى بها الأقلام في غاية الحدة وان تكون براية القلم على شكل
منقار الكركي محرفا من الجانب الايمن، وينبغي أن يكون المقط الذي يقط عليه
في غاية الصلابة، ويجب أن تكون الانقاش فارسية خفيفة الوزن والكاغد صقيلا
متساويا وان يجوز مده لانه يتوحش بذلك الخط وأن تكون صور الحروف يشبه بعضها
بعضا ولا يقدر ذلك إلا حكيم عاقل أو من تعودت بذلك أنامله.
وكان عبد الله بن رافع كاتبا لامير المؤمنين علي بن  أبي طالب كرم الله
وجهه فقال كنت أكتب يوما فقال لي أمير المؤمنين ألق دواتك وأطل جلفة قلمك
ووسع ما بين السطور واجمع ما بين الحروف وكان عبد الله بن جبلة كاتبا محسنا
فقال لغلمانه لتكون أقلامكم بحرية فإن لم تكن بحرية فلتكن صفرا واقطعوا عقد
الأقلام لئلا تنعقد الأمور، ولا يجوز انفاذ كتاب بغير ختم فإن كرم الكتاب
ختمه.
وقال عبد الله بن عباس في تفسير قوله تعالى: (أني ألقي إلي كتاب كريم) .
أي مختوم. وأمر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يكتب كتابا إلى العجم وقال
انهم لا يريدون كتابا بغير ختم فختمه بخاتمه المبارك وكان عليه ثلاثة أسطر
محمد رسول الله. خبر روى صخر بن عمرو أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لما
كتب كتابا إلى النجاشي
رماه على التراب ثم أنفذه فلا جرم أنه أسلم. ولما كتب كتابا إلى كسرى
أنوشروان لم يلقه على التراب لا جرم أنه لم يسلم وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم
تربوا كتبكم فإنه أنجح لحوائجكم. وقال تربوا الكتاب فإن التراب مبارك وإذا
كتب الكتاب فليقرأ قبل طيه فإن رأى فيه خطأ تدراكه وأصلحه. وينبغي أن يجتهد
الكاتب أن يكون الكلام قصيرا والمعنى طويلا، وأن لا يكرر كلمة يكتبها، وأن
يحترز من الألفاظ الثقيلة الغثة ليكون كاتبها محمودا. وفي باب الكتابة كلام
طويل كثير ان ذكرناه طال الكتاب ونقتنع منه بهذا القدر فقد قيل خير الكلام
ما قل ودل وجل ولم يمل.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ل-م (q-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The reed pen; originally a trimmed reed used for writing; extended to any writing instrument.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The pen as the instrument of divine inscription and human knowledge transmission; symbol of recorded wisdom.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for the writing implement; metaphorical (majāz) for the faculty of knowledge and decree.
- Root: ك-ت-ب (k-t-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To write, to inscribe, to prescribe; the act of gathering letters into a composed form.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Writing as the preservation of knowledge against the ravages of time; the scribe (kātib) as one who fixes meaning in durable form.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for inscribing; metaphorical for divine decree (kitāb) and obligation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — careful parsing of "if not for the sword and the pen, the world would not have advanced" to distinguish necessary condition from temporal sequence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The scholars have declared that nothing is more excellent than the pen, for through it the past and the bygone can be restored.

Among the merits and honors of the pen is that God—mighty and majestic is He—swore by it, saying, He who is exalted in glory: {«Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe»} (68:1). And He, exalted is He, said: {«Recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous—He who taught by the pen, taught man what he knew not»} (96:3–5). And the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The first thing God—exalted is He—created was the pen, and it ran with what shall be until the Day of Resurrection"—the hadith.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās said regarding the interpretation of this verse—narrating from Joseph, peace be upon him: {«Set me over the treasuries of the earth; indeed, I am a knowing guardian»} (12:55). He said: Its meaning is "a scribe and an accountant." And he said: The pen is the smith of speech.

A wisdom: Ibn al-Muʿtazz said: The pen is a mine, and the intellect is a jewel; the pen is the smith, and calligraphy is the craft. Galen said: The pen is the physician of speech. Balīnās said: The pen is a great talisman. Alexander said: The world lies under two things—the sword and the pen; and the sword lies under the pen. The pen is the discipline of the learned and their merchandise; by it is known the opinion of every man, near and far. And however experienced a man may be with time, unless he looks into books, he will not be complete in intellect—for the duration of a man's life is finite, and it is also known that within this short span, and with a brief lifetime, how much he can grasp through his own experience; and it is likewise known how much he can retain in his heart. The sword and the pen are two rulers over all things; and were it not for the sword and the pen, the world would not have advanced.

As for the scribes, it is not permissible for them to know more than the limits of writing, so that they may be fit for the service of the great. And the sages and ancient kings have said: The scribe ought to be learned in ten things. First: the distance of water and its proximity beneath the earth; and knowledge of extracting legal opinions (istiftāʾ); and knowledge of the increase and decrease of night and day in summer and winter; and the courses of the sun, the moon, and the stars; and knowledge of conjunction (ijtimāʿ) and opposition (istiqbāl); and reckoning by the fingers; and the science of geometry; and the calendar (taqwīm); and the choices of days (ikhtiyārāt al-ayyām) and what befits farmers; and knowledge of medicine and remedies; and knowledge of the south wind and the north wind; and the science of poetry and rhymes. And with all this, the scribe ought to be light of spirit, pleasant in meeting, learned in the trimming of the pen, its management, its cutting, its lifting, and its script. And whatever is in his heart, he should manifest it with the point of his pen; and he should guard himself against being scattered or disjointed. And the script should be well-founded, giving every letter its due—as it is narrated that a governor of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—may God be pleased with him—wrote a letter to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ in which he did not show the sīn of "In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate." So ʿAmr summoned him and said: First show the sīn of "In the name of God," and then proceed to your office.

And the first thing the scribe ought to learn is the trimming of the pen; for if a man writes well and knows how to trim his pen, the script will in any case come out sound.

A narrative: The Shāhanshāh had ten viziers, and among their company was the Ṣāḥib Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbbād. The viziers gathered to demean him and agreed to slander him, saying: The Ṣāḥib cannot even trim his pen. When the Shāhanshāh learned of this, he gathered them, and they said: "The Ṣāḥib—what adab is there in any of you like mine, that you dare to speak of me in the presence of the Shāhanshāh? My father taught me the vizierate, not commerce. The least of my adab is the trimming of the pen. Is there any among you who can write a complete letter with a pen whose head is broken?" The group was silenced by this. Then the Shāhanshāh said to him: "You write." So the Ṣāḥib took a pen, broke its head, and wrote with it a complete scroll. The group acknowledged his excellence and confessed his rectitude and nobility.

The finest pens are those that are straight, yellow in color, and thin in the middle. The pen beveled from its right side suits the Arabic, Persian, and Hebrew scripts. As for the Darī tongue, its pen must be beveled from the left side. The best of pens is that described by Yaḥyā ibn Jaʿfar al-Barmakī in a letter he wrote to Yaḥyā ibn Layth: "A pen neither thick nor thin, with a delicate middle." The knife with which pens are trimmed must be extremely sharp, and the trimming of the pen should be in the shape of a crane's beak, beveled from the right side. The cutting block (miqaṭṭ) upon which one cuts should be extremely hard. The engraving (inqāsh) should be Persian, light in weight, and the paper polished and even; and it is permissible to moisten it, for the script becomes wild otherwise. The forms of the letters should resemble one another—and none can achieve this save a wise, intelligent man, or one whose fingers have become accustomed to it.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rāfiʿ was a scribe for the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—may God honor his face. He said: I was writing one day, and the Commander of the Faithful said to me: "Lengthen your inkwell, extend the shaft of your pen, widen the space between the lines, and bring the letters close together." And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jabalah was an excellent scribe, and he said to his servants: "Let your pens be sea-like (baḥriyyah); if they are not sea-like, then let them be yellow. And cut the knots of the pens, lest affairs become knotted." And it is not permissible to dispatch a letter without a seal, for the honor of a letter is its seal.

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās said regarding the interpretation of the saying of God, exalted is He: {«Indeed, there has been cast to me a noble letter»} (27:29)—that is, sealed. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded that a letter be written to the non-Arabs, and he said: "They will not accept a letter without a seal." So he sealed it with his blessed seal, upon which were three lines: "Muḥammad, the Messenger of God."

A report: Ṣakhr ibn ʿAmr narrated that when the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, wrote a letter to the Negus, he cast it upon the earth and then dispatched it—and for that very reason he embraced Islam. And when he wrote a letter to Khusraw Anūshirwān, he did not cast it upon the earth—and for that reason he did not embrace Islam. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Earth your letters, for it is more successful for your needs." And he said: "Earth the letter, for the earth is blessed." And when a letter is written, it should be read before folding; if a mistake is found in it, one should overtake it and correct it.

And the scribe ought to strive that the speech be short and the meaning long, and that he not repeat a word he writes, and that he guard against heavy, coarse expressions—so that its writer may be praiseworthy. On the subject of writing there is much lengthy discourse; were we to mention it, the book would grow long. We content ourselves with this much, for it has been said: The best speech is that which is little yet indicative, noble yet not wearisome.

- Root: ب-و-ب (b-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A gate, door, or entryway; also a chapter or section of a book, derived from the notion of an opening through which one passes into a larger structure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In scholarly and theological usage, a chapter (bāb) signifies a distinct thematic division of knowledge, akin to a portal into a discipline’s deeper rulings and principles.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — a physical door; metaphorical (majāz) — a section of discourse, as the mind "enters" a topic through it.
